content:
The Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China and its former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan, former vice-chairmen Albert Ho and Chow Hang-tung are charged with "inciting subversion of state power." The Alliance, Lee and Chow pleaded not guilty and were convicted last Friday. The defendants, together with Ho who pleaded guilty earlier, submitted mitigation pleas today (the 28th). Senior counsel Simon Shen, representing Lee and Ho, argued in his sentencing submission that their cases should fall under "lesser circumstances," as "End one-party dictatorship" was merely propaganda and a slogan, with no concrete plans, guidelines, roadmaps or timelines. The judge at one point said the case was "closer to" the 47 defendants case and asked the defence which was more serious. Shen said the two cases were significantly different — the 47 case involved a very clear plan with a roadmap, while the Alliance's audience each practised their own way, "not knowing what actual action they were being incited to take." The court adjourned sentencing to within two weeks. Related reports: Alliance case mitigation | Chow Hang-tung does not mitigate: At peace with myself, no crime to regret — submissions repeatedly interrupted by judge Alliance case mitigation | Chow Hang-tung does not mitigate — uploads "My Plea Statement" on Patreon Alliance case mitigation — outside court | Queue party members litter again, stopped by police — "Female Long Hair" searched, belongings photographed item by item

Lee Cheuk-yan's wife Tang Yin-ngo left when the court rose, saying she would "continue to keep hope and continue to pray."

Senior counsel representing Lee Cheuk-yan and Albert Ho says "End one-party dictatorship" is an empty slogan

Senior counsel Simon Shen, representing Lee Cheuk-yan and Albert Ho, made oral supplementary submissions on sentencing, first reiterating that sentencing should only consider the indictment period, namely approximately 14 months from 1 July 2020 to September 2021, with prior conduct being merely background information.

He then pointed out that the court's verdict accepted that all defendants had for years used only peaceful, non-violent means for propaganda, proving the case was "very different" from those involving violence or incitement to violence. This case differed from others in that there was no plan or incitement to substantive acts; all the defendants' conduct, according to the conviction, was merely propaganda and slogans, without any concrete plans, guidelines, roadmaps or even timelines, "Viewed from this angle, those six characters, 'End one-party dictatorship,' are a slogan — one that, as I say, in hindsight, is an empty slogan."

Judge says case is closer to 47 defendants case — asks which is more serious

Judge Amanda Li said that, setting aside incitement, this case might be closer to the 47 case, and asked which was more serious when compared. Shen said the two were significantly different: in the 47 case, the defendants conspired to indiscriminately veto the budget after being elected, making the entire plan and conduct "very clear and with a roadmap," whereas this case had no roadmap or timeline, with the audience each practising their own way, "not knowing what actual action they were being incited to take."

Shen continued that substantive damage and impact caused by the incitement offence was an important sentencing factor, and clearly after all these years, no evidence could be seen showing "any Hong Kong resident or any matter where the goal was achieved through incitement of this kind by the Alliance." For over 30 years of incitement, not a single matter or person had undermined the fundamental system under the Chinese Constitution because of the Alliance's propaganda — "the Communist Party has remained very stable all these years" and continued to fulfil its duties.

He also pointed out that the prosecution insisted on charging two independent elements — "overthrowing and undermining the fundamental system of China established by the Constitution" and "overthrowing the central state power organs" — with the latter ultimately not established, and that this case merely involved propaganda slogans, with no substantive undermining of central state power or organs. Li also noted that the prosecution had acknowledged the two bases of charge would affect sentencing: if both were established it would be more serious, if not established it would be less serious.

Senior counsel Simon Shen, representing Lee Cheuk-yan and Albert Ho, argued that the defendants' offences fall under "lesser circumstances." (File photo)

Argument that unconstitutional conduct is a novel point — should fall under "lesser circumstances"

Additionally, Shen said the court convicted the defendants on the basis that their propaganda conduct undermined the fundamental system of China in accordance with the Constitution, and was impermissible under the Constitution, and "this point is actually novel," arrived at through argument between prosecution and defence and the court's consideration. Li said he understood, noting "before this case, none of us had thought that even this could be illegal," but pointed out that a similar situation was encountered in the 47 case, where because the law was relatively new and defendants might not understand the law, "some reduction was given," though the Court of Appeal said that aspect should not warrant a reduction.

Shen responded that it was a matter of degree, pointing out that after the National Security Law, everyone had to comply with the new law, but Lee and Ho were not legal experts; if the new law contained very important constitutional points that ordinary people, including Alliance officers and members of the public, would not understand, this should be an important mitigating factor, and different in degree from the 47 case. He also said the provisions of the National Security Law do not show that any interpretation of the Chinese Constitution could achieve such a ruling, and asked the court to consider these factors in finding the defendants' cases to be of "lesser circumstances," meaning imprisonment of 5 years or below; even if found to be "serious circumstances," meaning 5 to 10 years' imprisonment, the sentence should be at the lowest end of that range.

Albert Ho pleaded guilty after committal proceedings — court says maximum 25% sentence reduction

Li also raised concerns about Ho's health. Shen said he visited Ho frequently, noting that Ho's condition was stable after cancer treatment and he still needed to continue taking medication, but there was "nothing particularly special," and noted Ho is currently 74 and will turn 75 in December this year, asking the court to consider this.

Li continued to raise concerns, noting the defence's submission said that because Ho pleaded guilty, he should receive the full one-third discount for guilty plea, but the court understood that only pleading guilty during committal proceedings entitled one to a one-third discount; if pleading guilty after committal proceedings but before a confirmed trial date, only 20% to 25% discount should apply. Shen said this case was special — after committal proceedings were completed, Ho had indicated an intention to plead guilty around mid-2025, after which the court had adjourned the trial several times, hoping for a discretionary reduction exceeding 25%.

Judge Jolie Lai said according to court records, the case was committed to the High Court in September 2022, with three pre-trial reviews conducted in 2024, and the judge first notified the trial dates in September of that year — all occurring before 2025. Li reiterated that precedents state only guilty pleas at or before committal proceedings receive the full one-third discount. Shen reiterated it was a matter of discretion, asking the court to consider that the case took a very long time to reach trial and grant the maximum reduction. He also said if the sentence was under 5 years, this issue was relatively unimportant, as Ho had already been remanded for three and a half years for this case; but if the sentence was 5 to 10 years, he hoped for the lowest sentence, although the most likely actual outcome was a five-year prison term.

Can public service reduce sentence? — judge uses metaphor of money box "running out of money"

Additionally, Li raised concerns about the defence's mention of Lee and Ho having served as legislators for long periods and having held public office, noting they had prior conviction records and asking whether mitigation for public service had already been applied in those cases. Shen responded, "I have never understood nor agreed that a person's historical public service can only be used once," giving examples of people who contributed to society for years or had good character as things one possesses that cannot be lost, and not unavailable simply because considered in other cases.

Li used the metaphor of a money box — if public service or good character is treated as a money box, doing good deeds stores money, committing offences takes money out, would there come a day when the money box "not only runs out but might be in the negative"? Shen said the metaphor was not quite appropriate, noting some cases had nothing to do with prior public service character, and judgment should be based on the nature of the offence. Judge Christopher Chan asked if a defendant were a habitual offender, would that be an aggravating factor. Shen said if one previously had good character but later became a habitual offender, that proved "the person has changed," and prior good character should no longer be considered; but in this case the defendants had served as Legislative Council members for 21 years and served the public for many years, unrelated to the political offence they committed. The defendants were not the kind of "hardcore" criminal offenders commonly seen in criminal courts, but had merely participated in the Alliance according to their own beliefs and convictions, and their public service would not disappear because of prior unlawful assembly convictions.

Li said he understood, and reminded the public not to get the impression the court was calling the defendants "habitual offenders," only that it was convenient for discussion. Shen reiterated that this case and the 47 case "share the same crux — we are not dealing with hardcore criminals." Li concluded that regarding whether good character mitigation could not be used again because previously applied in prior convictions, the defence believed it depended on whether the defendant's fundamental character had changed, and asked the court to "think about it."

Additionally, before the court rose, Judge Chan raised concerns about the defence's mention of Section 10 of the Crimes Ordinance on sedition. Shen explained that if the court accepted that the main conduct was incitement without calling on anyone to take any action, and due to the constitutional interpretation, propaganda also became a criminal offence under the National Security Law, this basis of conviction would be similar to the old Section 10 sedition offence under the Crimes Ordinance — namely that no one needed to be called upon to do anything, mere spoken propaganda was enough to establish sedition. Shen noted that after Article 23 was passed, the old sedition offence was repealed and the maximum sentence under the new sedition offence was increased, but the characteristics of this case were similar to the old sedition offence, so he submitted that the old guidelines — 2 years' imprisonment for first offenders, 3 years for repeat offenders — were worth referencing.
